claim: The supraspinal connectome consists of numerous sensory, motor, and autonomic projections from brain to spinal cord.
source: The supraspinal connectome is essential for normal behavior and homeostasis and consists of numerous sensory, motor, and autonomic projections from brain to spinal cord.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract describing the supraspinal connectome, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Study of supraspinal control after damage has focused mostly on a handful of major populations that carry motor commands.
source: Study of supraspinal control and its restoration after damage has focused mostly on a handful of major populations that carry motor commands, with only limited consideration of dozens more that provide autonomic or crucial motor modulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction discussing the narrow focus of SCI research.

claim: Optimized viral labeling, 3D imaging, and registration to a mouse digital neuroanatomical atlas assigned tens of thousands of supraspinal neurons to 69 identified regions.
source: Optimized viral labeling, 3D imaging, and registration to a mouse digital neuroanatomical atlas assigned tens of thousands of supraspinal neurons to 69 identified regions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The supraspinal connectome is highly conserved in mammals.
source: The supraspinal connectome is highly conserved in mammals, with multiple cell types distributed through the brainstem, midbrain, and motor cortex, each projecting axons to a subset of spinal levels and to selected cell types (Nudo and Masterton, 1988; Kuypers and Martin, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on supraspinal connectivity across mammalian species.

claim: Multiple cell types in the supraspinal connectome are distributed through the brainstem, midbrain, and motor cortex.
source: The supraspinal connectome is highly conserved in mammals, with multiple cell types distributed through the brainstem, midbrain, and motor cortex, each projecting axons to a subset of spinal levels and to selected cell types (Nudo and Masterton, 1988; Kuypers and Martin, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on the anatomical distribution of supraspinal neurons.

claim: Each supraspinal cell type projects axons to a subset of spinal levels and to selected cell types.
source: The supraspinal connectome is highly conserved in mammals, with multiple cell types distributed through the brainstem, midbrain, and motor cortex, each projecting axons to a subset of spinal levels and to selected cell types (Nudo and Masterton, 1988; Kuypers and Martin, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on supraspinal projection patterns.

claim: Extensive work spanning more than a century has employed orthograde degeneration, electrical stimulation, and axonal transport-tracing methods to characterize supraspinal neurons.
source: Extensive work spanning more than a century has employed orthograde degeneration, electrical stimulation, and axonal transport-tracing methods to characterize the location and function of specific supraspinal neurons in various animals, providing a base of knowledge to understand supraspinal control (Nudo and Masterton, 1988; Kuypers and Martin, 1982; Hoff, 1932; Glees, 1946; ten Donkelaar, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to historical and foundational work in the field.

claim: Several efforts in rodents have provided global information by performing retrograde tracing from selected spinal levels, followed by tissue sectioning and manual assignment of labeled cell bodies to brain regions.
source: Several efforts in rodents have provided more global information by performing retrograde tracing from selected spinal levels, followed by tissue sectioning and manual assignment of labeled cell bodies to regions within the brain (Lakke, 1997; Leong et al., 1984; Liang et al., 1997 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior rodent studies using retrograde tracing methods.

claim: Information about the location and types of supraspinal neurons is fragmented and not standardized across numerous studies.
source: First, information about the location and types of supraspinal neurons is fragmented and not standardized across numerous studies (Tuszynski and Steward, 2012 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation discussing the fragmented nature of supraspinal research.

claim: A high level of expertise is required to precisely identify brain regions from two-dimensional tissue series and build a three-dimensional view of the connections.
source: Second, a high level of expertise is required to precisely identify brain regions from two-dimensional (2D) tissue series and build a three-dimensional (3D) view of the connections (Gong et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2014; Economo et al., 2016 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work on neuroanatomical mapping challenges.

claim: Tissue sectioning and imaging are laborious and time consuming, making experiments to track dynamic changes after injury or disease impractical.
source: Third, tissue sectioning and imaging are laborious and time consuming, making experiments to track dynamic changes after injury or disease impractical.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of traditional methods, based on general knowledge of histological techniques.

claim: In the field of spinal cord injury, the vast majority of studies concern only a handful of descending populations, notably the corticospinal, rubrospinal, raphespinal, and broadly defined reticulospinal.
source: For example, in the field of spinal cord injury (SCI), the vast majority of studies concern only a handful of descending populations, notably the corticospinal, rubrospinal, raphespinal, and broadly defined reticulospinal (Fink and Cafferty, 2016; Anderson, 2004; Kwon et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2012; Blackmore et al., 2021; Takakusaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to SCI research literature.

claim: Corticospinal, rubrospinal, raphespinal, and reticulospinal regions serve important motor functions and comprise a majority of descending input.
source: This attention is justified as these regions serve important motor functions and comprise a majority of descending input (Lemon, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to work on motor pathway functions.

claim: Dozens of additional brain regions also project to the spinal cord, many of which carry essential motor and autonomic commands.
source: On the other hand, dozens of additional brain regions also project to the spinal cord, many of which carry essential motor and autonomic commands (Liang et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to comprehensive anatomical work.

claim: Nuclear localization of mScarlet fluorophore significantly enhanced detection of supraspinal neurons in cleared brain tissue compared to cytoplasmic localization.
source: Indeed, 2 weeks after delivery of retrograde vectors to the lumbar spinal cord, detection of supraspinal neurons in cleared brain tissue was significantly enhanced when mScarlet (mSc) fluorophore (Bindels et al., 2017) was localized to the nucleus by an H2B tag (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nuclear-localized mScarlet resulted in an approximately 2-fold increase in detected cells in the cortex compared to cytoplasmic mScarlet.
source: Spot detection confirmed an approximately 2-fold increase in the number of detected cells in the cortex and more than 10-fold increase in the brainstem (249.6 ± 56.3 SEM vs. 3334.3 ± 82.8 SEM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nuclear-localized mScarlet resulted in more than 10-fold increase in detected cells in the brainstem compared to cytoplasmic mScarlet.
source: Spot detection confirmed an approximately 2-fold increase in the number of detected cells in the cortex and more than 10-fold increase in the brainstem (249.6 ± 56.3 SEM vs. 3334.3 ± 82.8 SEM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: H2B-mGreenLantern significantly increased detection of neurons in cortex, dorsal pons, and reticular formation compared to H2B-mScarlet.
source: Quantification of labeled objects revealed that H2B-mGL significantly increased detection of neurons in cortex, dorsal pons, and reticular formation (p<0.01, two-way ANOVA with post-hoc Sidak's) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2L–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Counts of retrogradely labeled neurons were similar in right and left hemispheres, confirming that spinal injections reached both sides equally.
source: Counts were similar in right and left hemispheres, confirming that spinal injections reached both sides equally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), and did not increase between 2 and 4 weeks post-injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Counts of retrogradely labeled neurons did not increase between 2 and 4 weeks post-injection.
source: Counts were similar in right and left hemispheres, confirming that spinal injections reached both sides equally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), and did not increase between 2 and 4 weeks post-injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: H2B-mGreenLantern signal was readily detectable without the need for antibody amplification.
source: Moreover, signal was readily detectable without the need for antibody amplification, thus avoiding lengthy incubation periods.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental procedures described.

claim: On average, 31,219 nuclei were detected per brain after lumbar injection of AAV2-retro-H2B-mGL.
source: On average, 31,219 nuclei were detected per brain (range 20,688–40,171).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Supraspinal nuclei were detected in 69 of the 645 total brain regions.
source: Supraspinal nuclei were detected in 69 of the 645 total brain regions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: The largest group of supraspinal neurons in the medulla registered to the gigantocellular nucleus.
source: In the medulla, the largest group of supraspinal neurons registered to the gigantocellular nucleus (GRN), an evolutionarily conserved source of both pre-autonomic and pre-motor axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B8; Aicher et al., 1995; Brownstone and Chopek, 2018; Liang et al., 2016; Hermann et al., 2003 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work on the gigantocellular nucleus.

claim: The gigantocellular nucleus is an evolutionarily conserved source of both pre-autonomic and pre-motor axons.
source: In the medulla, the largest group of supraspinal neurons registered to the gigantocellular nucleus (GRN), an evolutionarily conserved source of both pre-autonomic and pre-motor axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B8; Aicher et al., 1995; Brownstone and Chopek, 2018; Liang et al., 2016; Hermann et al., 2003 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on the gigantocellular nucleus.

claim: Labeled nuclei were present in the magnocellular reticular nucleus, which projects to the ventral horn and IML of the lower spinal cord.
source: More ventrally, labeled nuclei were present in the magnocellular reticular nucleus (MARN), which also project to the ventral horn and IML of the lower spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and general knowledge of the magnocellular reticular nucleus.

claim: Labeled nuclei mapped to regions lateral to the GRN, including the paragigantocellular reticular nucleus, lateral part.
source: Notably, labeled nuclei also mapped to regions lateral to the GRN, including the paragigantocellular reticular nucleus, lateral part (PGRNl) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B10).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The paragigantocellular reticular nucleus, lateral part contains spinally projecting neurons that may initiate locomotion.
source: This region contains spinally projecting neurons that may initiate locomotion, as well as the ventral rostral medullary group that regulates blood pressure (Capelli et al., 2017; Van Bockstaele et al., 1989; Opris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the paragigantocellular reticular nucleus.

claim: The paragigantocellular reticular nucleus, lateral part contains the ventral rostral medullary group that regulates blood pressure.
source: This region contains spinally projecting neurons that may initiate locomotion, as well as the ventral rostral medullary group that regulates blood pressure (Capelli et al., 2017; Van Bockstaele et al., 1989; Opris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on blood pressure regulation.

claim: A cluster of labeled nuclei was located dorsally in the caudal medulla, within and near the solitary nucleus.
source: A cluster of labeled nuclei was also located dorsally in the caudal medulla, within and near the solitary nucleus, as supraspinal region implicated in visceral input to respiration and cardiovascular tone (Leong et al., 1984; Liang et al., 1997; Mtui et al., 1995 ; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: The solitary nucleus is implicated in visceral input to respiration and cardiovascular tone.
source: A cluster of labeled nuclei was also located dorsally in the caudal medulla, within and near the solitary nucleus, as supraspinal region implicated in visceral input to respiration and cardiovascular tone (Leong et al., 1984; Liang et al., 1997; Mtui et al., 1995 ; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the solitary nucleus.

claim: Labeled nuclei were present in the spinal and medial vestibular nuclei, which project to spinal targets to mediate postural control.
source: More rostrally in the brainstem, labeled nuclei were present in the spinal and medial vestibular nuclei, which project to spinal targets to mediate postural control (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and general knowledge of vestibular function.

claim: Labeled nuclei were abundant in the pontine reticular nuclei.
source: Labeled nuclei were also abundant in the pontine reticular nuclei (Leong et al., 1984; Liang et al., 1997; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Pontine reticular neurons have been linked to muscle atonia during sleep, startle responses, and to multisegment postural adjustments during limb extension.
source: Although perhaps less well understood than medullary reticular populations, pontine reticular neurons have been linked to muscle atonia during sleep, startle responses, and to multisegment postural adjustments during limb extension (Perreault and Giorgi, 2019; Takakusaki et al., 2016 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on pontine reticular function.

claim: Labeled nuclei mapped to known supraspinal regions in and around the pontine central gray, including the locus coeruleus, laterodorsal and sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus.
source: More dorsally in the pons, labeled nuclei mapped to known supraspinal regions in and around the pontine central gray, including the locus coeruleus (LC), laterodorsal and sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (Leong et al., 1984; Liang et al., 1997 Cornwall et al., 1990; Peever and Fuller, 2016; Sluka and Westlund, 1992; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Labeled nuclei registered to Barrington's nucleus, which plays a central role in the control of micturition and bowel control.
source: Labeled nuclei also registered to Barrington's nucleus (BAR), which plays a central role in the control of micturition and bowel control (Barrington, 1921 Verstegen et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work on Barrington's nucleus.

claim: The parabrachial nucleus is a sensory relay for inputs related to itch, pain, touch, and a range of autonomic controls including blood pressure and thermoregulation.
source: Another prominent nucleus was the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), a sensory relay for inputs related to itch, pain, touch, and a range of autonomic controls including blood pressure and thermoregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B3; Chiang et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2020 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the parabrachial nucleus.

claim: Deep cerebellar nuclei project to lumbar spinal cord and were recently shown to retrogradely express lumbar-injected AAV2-retro.
source: Notably, although deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) project to lumbar spinal cord and were recently shown to retrogradely express lumbar-injected AAV2-retro (Sathyamurthy et al., 2020), detection of cell nuclei in this region was low and highly variable between animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on deep cerebellar nuclei.

claim: Detection of cell nuclei in deep cerebellar nuclei was low and highly variable between animals.
source: Notably, although deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) project to lumbar spinal cord and were recently shown to retrogradely express lumbar-injected AAV2-retro (Sathyamurthy et al., 2020), detection of cell nuclei in this region was low and highly variable between animals.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Supraspinal nuclei were prominently detected in the red nucleus in the midbrain.
source: In the midbrain, supraspinal nuclei were prominently detected in the RN, as expected, and in midline regions including Edinger–Westphal (EW) and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC), whose supraspinal projections are known to affect postural adjustments and energy homeostasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B; Leong et al., 1984 Yu and Wang, 2020; Kozicz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and general knowledge of the red nucleus.

claim: Supraspinal nuclei were detected in midline regions including Edinger–Westphal and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal, whose supraspinal projections are known to affect postural adjustments and energy homeostasis.
source: In the midbrain, supraspinal nuclei were prominently detected in the RN, as expected, and in midline regions including Edinger–Westphal (EW) and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC), whose supraspinal projections are known to affect postural adjustments and energy homeostasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B; Leong et al., 1984 Yu and Wang, 2020; Kozicz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on these nuclei.

claim: Nuclei mapped to the midbrain reticular nucleus and pedunculopontine nucleus, which lie within the mesencephalic locomotor region.
source: Interestingly, nuclei also mapped to the midbrain reticular nucleus and pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B2), which lie within the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), a well-studied region in which stimulation triggers locomotion in a range of species including mice (Caggiano et al., 2018; Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work on the mesencephalic locomotor region.

claim: The mesencephalic locomotor region is a well-studied region in which stimulation triggers locomotion in a range of species including mice.
source: Interestingly, nuclei also mapped to the midbrain reticular nucleus and pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B2), which lie within the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), a well-studied region in which stimulation triggers locomotion in a range of species including mice (Caggiano et al., 2018; Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the mesencephalic locomotor region.

claim: The presence of direct supraspinal input from the PPN and mesencephalic reticular nucleus indicates some role in direct spinal activation.
source: Although much MLR activity acts through reticular relays, the presence of direct supraspinal input from the PPN and mesencephalic reticular nucleus (MRN), noted here and elsewhere, indicates some role in direct spinal activation (Caggiano et al., 2018; Gatto and Goulding, 2018; Dautan et al., 2021; Ferreira-Pinto et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Large clusters of nuclei were detected in the corticospinal tract region in the forebrain.
source: Finally, in the forebrain, large clusters of nuclei were detected in the corticospinal tract region, as expected.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Supraspinal neurons were detected in the hypothalamus, where they separated into two prominent clusters, medial and lateral.
source: Supraspinal neurons were also detected in the hypothalamus, where they separated into two prominent clusters, medial and lateral (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B7).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The medial cluster of hypothalamic supraspinal neurons mapped mostly to the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus and the adjacent descending paraventricular nucleus.
source: The medial cluster mapped mostly to the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH) and the adjacent descending paraventricular nucleus (PVHd).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus and descending paraventricular nucleus innervate autonomic circuitry in the lower spinal cord and modulate functions including bladder control, sexual function, and blood pressure.
source: These are known to innervate autonomic circuitry in the lower spinal cord and modulate functions including bladder control, sexual function, and blood pressure (de Groat et al., 2015; Holstege, 2005; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus.

claim: The lateral cluster of hypothalamic supraspinal neurons spanned the dorsomedial nucleus and the lateral hypothalamic area.
source: The lateral cluster spanned the dorsomedial nucleus (DMH) and the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Prior work in the lateral hypothalamic area has identified orexin-expressing neurons that project to all spinal levels with functions that include pain modulation.
source: Although less well characterized than the PVH, prior work in the LHA has identified orexin-expressing neurons that project to all spinal levels with functions that include pain modulation (Swanson and Kuypers, 1980; van den Pol, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the lateral hypothalamic area.

claim: Compared to L1 injection, L4 and T10 injections showed no significant differences beyond a modest increase in CST and a modest decrease in GRN in T10-injected animals.
source: Interestingly, compared to L1 these cohorts showed no significant differences beyond a modest increase in CST and a modest decrease in GRN in T10-injected animals, highlighting the consistency of the approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The brain as a whole had an average lumbar projection index of just 26.5% (±2.6% SEM).
source: The brain as a whole had an average lumbar projection index of just 26.5% (±2.6% SEM), indicating a brain-wide tendency for many axons to terminate in cervical regions without continuing caudally to lumbar segments.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The brain shows a brain-wide tendency for many axons to terminate in cervical regions without continuing caudally to lumbar segments.
source: The brain as a whole had an average lumbar projection index of just 26.5% (±2.6% SEM), indicating a brain-wide tendency for many axons to terminate in cervical regions without continuing caudally to lumbar segments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the quantitative data on lumbar projection index.

claim: The medullary reticular formations and the parvocellular nucleus showed very low indexes of lumbar projection, indicating largely cervical termination.
source: The medullary reticular formations (MDRNd and MDRNv, located caudally to the gigantocellular reticular nuclei) and the laterally positioned parvocellular nucleus both showed very low indexes of lumbar projection, indicating largely cervical termination.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The medullary reticular formations have been recently implicated in forelimb-reaching behavior, a function that would be consistent with predominantly cervical projections.
source: Interestingly, these regions have been recently implicated in forelimb-reaching behavior, a function that would be consistent with predominantly cervical projections (Esposito et al., 2021; Ruder et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work on forelimb-reaching behavior.

claim: The 3D registration approach revealed an overall topographic pattern in the brainstem in which ventrally located populations projected to both lumbar and cervical regions, whereas more dorsally located populations rarely took up lumbar-injected label and were thus predominantly cervical.
source: The 3D registration approach also revealed an overall topographic pattern in the brainstem in which ventrally located populations projected to both lumbar and cervical regions, whereas more dorsally located populations rarely took up lumbar-injected label and were thus predominantly cervical (Figure 2B–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–G.

claim: The nucleus prepositus and Roller nucleus, dorsally located in the medulla, showed mostly cervical projections, possibly related to their known role in gaze tracking.
source: The nucleus prepositus and Roller nucleus, dorsally located in the medulla, showed mostly cervical projections, possibly related to their known role in gaze tracking (Figure 2N; Chiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to prior work on gaze tracking.

claim: The pontine reticular formations showed a more balanced distribution of lumbar and cervical projections.
source: In contrast, the pontine reticular formations showed a more balanced distribution.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The red nucleus was relatively balanced in lumbar and cervical projections but showed a topographic pattern in which ventral-medial neurons projected to lumbar cord.
source: The RN was also relatively balanced but showed a topographic pattern in which ventral-medial neurons projected to lumbar cord (Figure 2B–D; Wang et al., 2018; Flumerfelt and Gwyn, 1974; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work on red nucleus topography.

claim: Neurons near the pontine central gray, including Barrington's nucleus, showed relative enrichment for lumbar labeling, consistent with known innervation of lumbar circuitry.
source: Neurons near the pontine central gray, including Barrington's nucleus, showed relative enrichment for lumbar labeling, consistent with known innervation of lumbar circuitry (Figure 2E–G; Verstegen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to prior work on Barrington's nucleus.

claim: The paraventricular region of the hypothalamus was enriched for lumbar label, consistent with its known innervation of the IML cell column.
source: Similarly, the paraventricular region of the hypothalamus was enriched for lumbar label, consistent with its known innervation of the IML cell column.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and general knowledge of the paraventricular hypothalamus.

claim: In the deep cerebellar nuclei, only 8.5% (±1.0% SEM) of lumbar-projecting cells co-expressed cervical mScarlet.
source: For example, consistent with a recent report (Sathyamurthy et al., 2020), in the DCN only 8.5% (±1.0% SEM) of lumbar-projecting cells co-expressed cervical mScarlet.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data, consistent with a cited report.

claim: Only 14.4% (±2.5% SEM) of lumbar-projecting rubrospinal neurons expressed cervical mScarlet, consistent with established patterns of mostly segregated topography.
source: Similarly, only 14.4% (±2.5% SEM) of lumbar-projecting rubrospinal neurons expressed mSc, consistent with established patterns of mostly segregated topography (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data, consistent with established knowledge.

claim: The overall separation of mSc and mGL signal in the deep cerebellar nuclei and red nucleus indicates that fibers of passage in cervical spinal cord mostly failed to take up Retro-AAV2.
source: Importantly, the overall separation of mSc and mGL signal in these regions indicates that fibers of passage in cervical spinal cord mostly failed to take up Retro-AAV2, supporting prior conclusions by our lab and others that AAV2-retro is primarily taken up by collaterals or synaptic terminals (Wang et al., 2018; Steward et al., 2021; Sathyamurthy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AAV2-retro is primarily taken up by collaterals or synaptic terminals.
source: Importantly, the overall separation of mSc and mGL signal in these regions indicates that fibers of passage in cervical spinal cord mostly failed to take up Retro-AAV2, supporting prior conclusions by our lab and others that AAV2-retro is primarily taken up by collaterals or synaptic terminals (Wang et al., 2018; Steward et al., 2021; Sathyamurthy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on AAV2-retro uptake mechanisms.

claim: In the lateral hypothalamic area, 54.8% (±4.3% SEM) of lumbar-projecting neurons co-expressed cervical mScarlet.
source: In striking contrast, other brain regions displayed rates of mSc signal in lumbar-labeled neurons that approached the levels we measured with direct co-injection, for example, the LHA (54.8% [±4.3% SEM]) and gigantocellular reticular formation (48.5% [±2.5% SEM]) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: In the gigantocellular reticular formation, 48.5% (±2.5% SEM) of lumbar-projecting neurons co-expressed cervical mScarlet.
source: In striking contrast, other brain regions displayed rates of mSc signal in lumbar-labeled neurons that approached the levels we measured with direct co-injection, for example, the LHA (54.8% [±4.3% SEM]) and gigantocellular reticular formation (48.5% [±2.5% SEM]) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Lumbar-projecting neurons were absent from the lateral S2 and the more rostral forelimb area in the cortex.
source: In the cortex, as expected, lumbar-projecting neurons were absent from the lateral S2 and the more rostral forelimb area (RFA) and instead were concentrated in a subregion of M1, centered medial and caudal to the main mass of cervically labeled neurons (Steward et al., 2021; Sahni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, consistent with cited reports.

claim: Lumbar-projecting neurons were concentrated in a subregion of M1, centered medial and caudal to the main mass of cervically labeled neurons.
source: In the cortex, as expected, lumbar-projecting neurons were absent from the lateral S2 and the more rostral forelimb area (RFA) and instead were concentrated in a subregion of M1, centered medial and caudal to the main mass of cervically labeled neurons (Steward et al., 2021; Sahni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, consistent with cited reports.

claim: A rim of cervically labeled cells completely surrounded the lumbar region in the cortex.
source: Interestingly, a rim of cervically labeled cells completely surrounded the lumbar region (Figure 2O, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Lumbar-projecting CST neurons can be described most accurately not as a separate caudal or medial population, but rather as nested within a broader region of cervical-projecting neurons.
source: Thus, lumbar-projecting CST neurons can be described most accurately not as a separate caudal or medial population, but rather as nested within a broader region of cervical-projecting neurons (Steward et al., 2021; Sahni et al., 2021 ).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Of the CST neurons that projected to lumbar cord, 53.0% (±3.0% SEM) were also labeled from cervical, indicating dual projection.
source: Importantly, this region also contained mSc-labeled neurons, and of the neurons that projected to lumbar cord 53.0% (±3.0% SEM) were also labeled from cervical, indicating dual projection (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Compared to neurons that project exclusively to cervical cord, neurons detected as dual-projecting showed significantly lower intensity of cervical mSc.
source: We noticed, however, that the cervically derived label was often very dim in dual-labeled cells. Indeed, quantification confirmed that compared to neurons that project exclusively to cervical cord, neurons detected as dual-projecting showed significantly lower intensity of cervical mSc (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The mGL signal averaged higher in dual-labeled neurons than in mGL-only cells.
source: Unlike the mSc signal, however, the mGL signal averaged higher in dual-labeled neurons than in mGL-only cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Dual-labeled neurons from co-injected control animals showed higher average intensity than single-labeled neurons and a positive correlation in the brightness of the two fluorophores.
source: Moreover, dual-labeled neurons from co-injected control animals showed higher average intensity than single-labeled neurons and a positive correlation in the brightness of the two fluorophores (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H and I).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Cross-suppression of expression is not a general feature of co-delivered AAV2-retro.
source: Thus, cross-suppression of expression is not a general feature of co-delivered AAV2-retro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on dual-labeled neurons.

claim: One possible explanation for dim cervical label in lumbar-projecting neurons is that viral uptake is proportional to synapse density, and the dim cervical label reflects collateralization in cervical cord that is present but sparse.
source: As discussed more fully later (see 'Discussion'), one possible explanation is that viral uptake is proportional to synapse density, and the dim cervical label in lumbar-projecting neurons reflects collateralization in cervical cord that is present but sparse.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors to interpret the data.

claim: Lumbar-projecting CST axons may send collaterals to cervical targets but at a density that is lower than in the lumbar cord, and also lower than CST neurons that project only to cervical cord.
source: The model that retrograde labeling is proportional to the amount of innervation would predict that lumbar-projecting CST axons may send collaterals to cervical targets but at a density that is lower than in the lumbar cord, and also lower than CST neurons that project only to cervical cord. Indeed, this is the pattern reported for CST neurons by anterograde tracing in two recent studies (Steward et al., 2021; Sahni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a prediction based on a proposed model, supported by citations to recent anterograde tracing studies.

claim: AAV2-retro effectively delivers transgenes to a wide diversity of cell types in the chronic phase of injury.
source: These data quantitatively verify AAV2-retro's ability to effectively deliver transgenes to a wide diversity of cell types in the chronic phase of injury, meeting an important perquisite for eventual translation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on chronic injury.

claim: In all brain regions examined, nuclei counts after chronic injury did not differ significantly from those found in uninjured animals with similar thoracic injections.
source: In cleared brains, examination of retrograde mGL showed a broad distribution of signal (Figure 4C–G), and in all regions the nuclei counts did not differ significantly from those found previously in uninjured animals with similar thoracic injections (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data comparing injured and uninjured animals.

claim: Mild injuries displayed elevated GFAP at the crush site but overall astrocytic continuity (92.5% ± 2.0 SEM).
source: As expected, mild injuries displayed elevated GFAP at the crush site but overall astrocytic continuity (92.5% ± 2.0 SEM) (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data on injury severity.

claim: Severe injuries completely abolished astrocytic continuity in two animals and reduced the third to 0.73% of initial.
source: Severe injuries completely abolished astrocytic continuity in two animals and reduced the third to 0.73% of initial.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data on injury severity.

claim: Moderate injury produced a significant reduction in astrocytic bridging compared to mild injury (32.2%±7.0 SEM, p=0.005 ANOVA with post-hoc Sidak's).
source: Moderate injury produced a significant reduction in astrocytic bridging compared to mild injury (32.2%±7.0 SEM, p=0.005 ANOVA with post-hoc Sidak's) but with considerable variability (range 8.4–75.4%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Mice that received severe injuries showed a maximum of 29 labeled cells brain-wide, confirming disruption of descending axon tracts.
source: Mice that received severe injuries showed a maximum of 29 labeled cells brain-wide, confirming disruption of descending axon tracts (Figure 5J, M and N).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data on severe injury.

claim: Mild injuries averaged only a 43% reduction in retrograde label, with high variability between different supraspinal populations.
source: In contrast, mild injuries averaged only a 43% reduction in retrograde label, with high variability between different supraspinal populations (Figure 5H, K and N).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data on mild injury.

claim: After mild injury, the CST was strongly affected, averaging less than 20% sparing, while neurons near the pontine central gray and the RN averaged 83.3 and 75.1% sparing, respectively.
source: For example, the CST was strongly affected, averaging less than 20% sparing, while neurons near the pontine central gray and the RN averaged 83.3 and 75.1% sparing, respectively (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data on region-specific sparing.

claim: The moderate injury group showed a brain-wide average of 24.2% sparing, with high variability between animals (range 3.4–36.3%).
source: The moderate injury group showed a brain-wide average of 24.2% sparing, also with high variability between animals (range 3.4–36.3%) (Figure 5I, L and N).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data on moderate injury.

claim: BMS scores averaged lower in animals that received severe injury versus moderate or mild.
source: As expected, BMS scores averaged lower in animals that received severe injury versus moderate or mild (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral data.

claim: Of the 12 animals, 4 recovered to a level of consistent plantar stepping (BMS ≥ 5), whereas 8 animals displayed no or infrequent stepping (BMS ≤ 3.5).
source: Of the 12 animals, 4 recovered to a level of consistent plantar stepping (BMS ≥ 5), whereas 8 animals displayed no or infrequent stepping (BMS ≤ 3.5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral data.

claim: Sparing in the pedunculopontine region differed significantly between impaired and high-performing groups, with the most damaged animal in the high-performing group exceeding the maximum value in the impaired group.
source: In contrast, sparing in supraspinal neurons located in the dorsal pontine region, most notably the pedunculopontine region, differed significantly between the two groups, with the most damaged animal in the high-performing group exceeding the maximum value in the impaired group (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data correlating sparing with function.

claim: The number of spared neurons in the cervical spinal cord differed significantly between impaired and high-performing groups and showed the widest gap between the maximum impaired value and the minimum high-performing value.
source: Interestingly, the number of spared neurons in the cervical spinal cord also differed significantly and showed the widest gap between the maximum impaired value and the minimum high-performing value, thus highlighting the potential importance of cervical neurons as a supralumbar control center (Zholudeva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data correlating sparing with function.

claim: The current approach detects a direct projection from the PPN to the lumbar spinal cord and a high correlation between maintenance of this pathway with locomotor function after SCI.
source: As one example, our data detect a direct projection from the PPN and the lumbar spinal cord and a high correlation between maintenance of this pathway with locomotor function after SCI.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental findings.

claim: The PPN lies within the MLR, an area that has been recognized for more than 50 years as an important area for locomotion.
source: Interestingly, the PPN lies within the MLR, an area that has been recognized for more than 50 years as an important area for locomotion (Gatto and Goulding, 2018; Shik et al., 1969 ) but which has received limited attention in SCI research.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on the MLR.

claim: The MLR has received limited attention in SCI research.
source: Interestingly, the PPN lies within the MLR, an area that has been recognized for more than 50 years as an important area for locomotion (Gatto and Goulding, 2018; Shik et al., 1969 ) but which has received limited attention in SCI research.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, based on general knowledge.

claim: The correlational analysis raises the hypothesis that in addition to rubrospinal and reticulospinal projection, the maintenance and regeneration of PPN-spinal projections may impact locomotor recovery from spinal injury.
source: Thus, the correlational analysis presented here raises the hypothesis that in addition to rubrospinal and reticulospinal projection, the maintenance and regeneration of PPN-spinal projections may impact locomotor recovery from spinal injury.
evidence: This is a hypothesis generated from the correlational data.

claim: The crush model does not mimic the acute impact involved in most human injuries.
source: First, although the crush model has been used to assess axon regeneration in the mouse (Liu et al., 2010; Leibinger et al., 2021; Brommer et al., 2021 Du et al., 2015), it must be acknowledged that it does not mimic the acute impact involved in most human injuries.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by citations to prior use of the crush model.

claim: Spinal contusion can leave an outer rim of spared tissue, which may favor residual brainstem–spinal connectivity.
source: For example, it was noted previously that spinal contusion can leave an outer rim of spared tissue, which may favor residual brainstem–spinal connectivity (Asboth et al., 2021 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on contusion models.

claim: AAV2-retro appears less effective at transducing serotonergic cell types, thereby limiting the assessment of raphe-spinal projections.
source: A third caveat regards viral tropism, for example, AAV2-retro appears less effective at transducing serotonergic cell types, thereby limiting the assessment of raphe-spinal projections (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on AAV2-retro tropism.

claim: The process of image registration smooths and obscures volumetric differences in brain regions.
source: Fourth, it is important to note that brain injury and disease can potentially alter the size of individual brain regions, but that the process of image registration smooths and obscures these differences (Niedworok et al., 2016 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on image registration limitations.

claim: The workflow is not suited to detect region-specific volumetric changes.
source: Thus, the workflow here is not suited to detect region-specific volumetric changes, and care should be taken in interpreting the results of registration in areas where large changes may have occurred.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the registration process.
